specStatements.text: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Rusting is an example of corrosion. Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.
Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier, such as greasing, painting or electroplating. Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.
Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection, eg zinc is used to galvanise iron.
Students should be able to:
describe experiments and interpret results to show that both air and water are necessary for rusting
explain sacrificial protection in terms of relative reactivity.
Most metals in everyday use are alloys.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc. The proportion of gold in the alloy is measured in carats. 24 carat being 100% (pure gold), and 18 carat being 75% gold.

Steels are alloys of iron that contain specific amounts of carbon and other metals. High carbon steel is strong but brittle. Low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped. Steels containing chromium and nickel (stainless steels) are hard and resistant to corrosion.
Aluminium alloys are low density.
Students should be able to:
recall a use of each of the alloys specified
interpret and evaluate the composition and uses of alloys other than those specified given appropriate information.

Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone. Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating in a furnace.

The properties of polymers depend on what monomers they are made from and the conditions under which they are made. For example, low density (LD) and high density (HD) poly(ethene) are produced from ethene.
Thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated. Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated.
Students should be able to:
explain how low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene
explain the difference between thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers in terms of their structures.
Most composites are made of two materials, a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material, which is called the reinforcement.
Students should be able to recall some examples of composites.
Students should be able to, given appropriate information:
compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals
explain how the properties of materials are related to their uses and select appropriate materials.

scopeNotes.statement: Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier, such as greasing, painting or electroplating.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the barrier methods the specification names are used - greasing, painting and electroplating - alongside the reactive coatings of the next statement. Electroplating is treated purely as a way of laying down a protective layer of another metal; half equations, electrode products and cell arrangements belong to 4.3 and are never required here. No equation for rusting is stated or expected, because the specification states none in this section.

scopeNotes.statement: The proportion of gold in the alloy is measured in carats. 24 carat being 100% (pure gold), and 18 carat being 75% gold.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Carats are handled exactly as the specification defines them: a measure of the proportion of gold, anchored on 24 carat = 100% and 18 carat = 75%. Any other carat figure appears only as arithmetic on that same scale (carats out of 24), and no student is asked to recall hallmarking rules or the exact proportions of silver, copper and zinc in a particular piece, none of which the specification supplies.

scopeNotes.statement: interpret and evaluate the composition and uses of alloys other than those specified given appropriate information.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Alloys beyond bronze, brass, gold alloys, the steels and aluminium alloys appear only in items that supply the composition and property data in the stem, honouring 'given appropriate information'. The composition of an unspecified alloy is never presented as something to memorise.

scopeNotes.statement: explain how low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The explanation is limited to what the specification supports: the same monomer, ethene, gives two different materials because different catalysts and different reaction conditions are used, since the properties of a polymer depend on its monomer and on the conditions of manufacture. Named industrial catalysts, temperatures and pressures are not stated by the specification and are not taught or examined here.

scopeNotes.statement: compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every quantitative comparison supplies its figures in the stem, as 'given appropriate information' requires. No density, melting point or strength value is ever something the student must recall; the skill assessed is reading supplied data and using it to choose between materials.

concepts.definition: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. It is a chemical change, not simply wear, and it is not confined to metals.
The corrosion of iron. It is one example of corrosion, and both air and water must be present for it to happen.
A layer applied to a metal that keeps air and water away from the surface, for example grease, paint or an electroplated layer of another metal.
Using electricity to deposit a thin layer of one metal onto the surface of another, used here as a way of applying a protective barrier.
The thin layer of oxide that forms on the surface of aluminium and protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.
Protecting a metal by putting it in contact with a more reactive metal, which corrodes in its place.
Coating iron or steel with zinc. The zinc acts as a barrier and, because it is more reactive than iron, also gives sacrificial protection.

concepts.term: Fair test in a rusting experiment
concepts.definition: Setting up tubes that differ in only one factor - air present or absent, water present or absent - so that any difference in rusting can be traced to that one factor.
A substance such as anhydrous calcium chloride that removes water vapour, used to give a nail air without water.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Most metals in everyday use are alloys because the mixture has more useful properties than the pure metal.
An alloy of copper and tin, used for statues, ornaments and bells.
An alloy of copper and zinc, used for musical instruments, door fittings and taps.
Gold mixed with silver, copper and zinc, which is harder and cheaper than pure gold.
The unit used for the proportion of gold in an alloy. 24 carat is 100% gold and 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron containing specific amounts of carbon and, in some steels, other metals.
Steel with a higher proportion of carbon. It is strong but brittle, so it is used for cutting tools and blades.
Steel with a lower proportion of carbon. It is softer and more easily shaped, so it is used for car bodies and sheeting.
Steel containing chromium and nickel. It is hard and resistant to corrosion, so it is used for cutlery, sinks and surgical tools.
An alloy of aluminium. Aluminium alloys are low density, so they are used for aircraft bodies and bicycle frames.
The glass in ordinary use, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide. It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
A material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.
The small molecule from which a polymer is built. Ethene is the monomer for poly(ethene).
Low density poly(ethene), made from ethene under one set of conditions with one catalyst. It is flexible and used for bags and bottles.
High density poly(ethene), made from the same monomer, ethene, but with a different catalyst and different conditions. It is stiffer and stronger.
A polymer made of separate tangled chains held to each other only by weak forces, so it melts when heated and can be reshaped.
A polymer whose chains are joined by cross-links. It does not melt when heated, so it keeps its shape at high temperature.
Strong bonds joining one polymer chain to another, which stop the chains moving past each other on heating.
A material made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a second material.
The material in a composite that surrounds and holds the reinforcement, for example the cement in concrete.
The fibres or fragments held inside the matrix of a composite, for example the gravel in concrete or the glass fibres in fibreglass.
Mass per unit volume. A low density material has a small mass for its size, which is why aluminium alloys suit aircraft.

misconceptions.question: A nail sits in a sealed tube of water with no air. Will it rust?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both air and water are necessary, so water on its own cannot rust iron.
misconceptions.misconception: Water is what makes iron rust, so anything wet rusts and the air plays no part.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every rusty object a student has seen was wet at some point, while air is invisible and always there, so it never registers as a variable that could be removed.
misconceptions.correction: A nail in water that has been boiled to drive off dissolved air and sealed under oil does not rust, even though it is soaking wet. The only thing missing is air, so air must be necessary too.

misconceptions.question: A nail sits in a tube of dry air over a drying agent. Will it rust?
misconceptions.correct: No. Water is necessary as well as air, so dry air cannot rust iron.
misconceptions.misconception: Rusting is just iron reacting with oxygen, so air alone is enough and water only speeds it up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rust is iron oxide, and the word oxide points straight to oxygen, so water looks like a helper rather than a necessity.
misconceptions.correction: The nail over anhydrous calcium chloride has all the air it needs and still does not rust. Rusting needs both, which is why the spec says both air and water are necessary.

misconceptions.question: Is corrosion another word for rusting?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rusting is one example of corrosion, the corrosion of iron.
misconceptions.misconception: Corrosion and rusting mean the same thing, so every corroding metal makes rust.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rust is the only corrosion product most students can name, so the specific example becomes a substitute for the general term.
misconceptions.correction: Copper corrodes to a green coating and aluminium corrodes to a white oxide. Neither is rust. Rust is what you get when it is iron that corrodes.

misconceptions.question: Can non-metals corrode?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Corrosion is the destruction of materials, not only of metals, by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.
misconceptions.misconception: Only metals can corrode, because corrosion means metal being eaten away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every classroom example is a metal, so the general definition gets quietly narrowed to metals.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines corrosion as the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Stone buildings attacked by acidic gases are corroding too.

misconceptions.question: A painted gate is scratched. Is the iron under the scratch still protected?
misconceptions.correct: No. A barrier coating only works while it is unbroken; a scratch lets air and water reach the iron.
misconceptions.misconception: A coat of paint goes on protecting the iron even where it has been chipped or scratched through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Barrier protection and sacrificial protection get merged into one idea called 'coating', so the property of one is credited to the other.
misconceptions.correction: Paint and grease work only by keeping air and water out. Break the layer and rusting starts at that spot, which is exactly why a reactive coating such as zinc is used where damage is likely.

misconceptions.question: Why does aluminium not corrode away in air?
misconceptions.correct: A layer of aluminium oxide forms on the surface and protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.
misconceptions.misconception: Aluminium is an unreactive metal, so air and water do not attack it at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Aluminium objects look clean and shiny for years, and 'does not corrode' is read as 'does not react', which contradicts its place in the reactivity series.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium is more reactive than iron. It reacts fast with oxygen, but the oxide it makes sticks to the surface as a tough layer that stops anything reaching the metal below.

misconceptions.question: Should the oxide layer be cleaned off aluminium before use?
misconceptions.correct: No. The oxide layer is what protects the metal, so it is left in place and is often deliberately thickened.
misconceptions.misconception: The oxide layer is corrosion damage and should be removed to leave clean bright metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxide layers on iron (rust) are flaky and harmful, so the same is assumed for every metal.
misconceptions.correction: Rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron; aluminium oxide does not. It is a continuous layer bonded to the surface, so removing it only lets a new one form.

misconceptions.question: How does a zinc coating protect iron?
misconceptions.correct: It acts as a barrier and, being more reactive than iron, also corrodes in the iron's place.
misconceptions.misconception: Zinc only works as a barrier, in the same way as a coat of paint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Zinc is applied as a coating, so it is filed with the barrier methods and its reactivity is never considered.
misconceptions.correction: The specification calls these coatings reactive. Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so even at a scratch the zinc reacts first and the iron is left alone.

misconceptions.question: Would a tin coating give iron sacrificial protection?
misconceptions.correct: No. Tin is less reactive than iron, so it protects only as a barrier, not sacrificially.
misconceptions.misconception: Any metal coating gives sacrificial protection; a less reactive metal is better because it resists corrosion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Resists corrosion' sounds like the property you want, so the less reactive metal seems the safer choice.
misconceptions.correction: Sacrificial protection needs a metal MORE reactive than the one being protected, so that it corrodes first. A scratched tin can rusts faster than bare iron, because iron is now the more reactive metal in contact with tin.

misconceptions.question: In galvanised iron, which metal is used up?
misconceptions.correct: The zinc is used up, because it is more reactive and corrodes in place of the iron.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron corrodes away and, in doing so, protects the zinc coating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'sacrificial' is attached to the object being protected rather than to the coating doing the protecting.
misconceptions.correction: The sacrifice is made BY the more reactive metal. Zinc corrodes and is slowly consumed; the iron underneath survives, which is the whole point.

misconceptions.question: In the rusting experiment the boiled water is covered with a layer of oil. What is the oil for?
misconceptions.correct: The oil keeps air out of the boiled water, so the nail has water but no air.
misconceptions.misconception: The oil is being tested as a protective coating on the nail.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oil is a barrier method in the very same topic, so it is read as the variable rather than as the seal that removes air.
misconceptions.correction: The oil never touches the nail; it floats on the water. Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil layer stops more dissolving back, so the only difference from the control is the absence of air.

misconceptions.question: Why is anhydrous calcium chloride put in the tube with the nail?
misconceptions.correct: It absorbs water vapour, so the nail is surrounded by air with no water present.
misconceptions.misconception: The calcium chloride is a chemical that coats the nail and stops it rusting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect any added chemical to act on the nail directly, rather than to change the air around it.
misconceptions.correction: The calcium chloride sits at the bottom of the tube, not on the nail. It is a drying agent: it removes water so that air can be tested on its own.

misconceptions.question: Is an alloy a compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements.
misconceptions.misconception: An alloy is a compound formed when two metals react and join together chemically.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Made from two metals' sounds like a chemical combination, and the everyday word 'mixture' feels too weak for something as solid as brass.
misconceptions.correction: There is no reaction and no fixed formula. The proportions can be varied, and the atoms are simply mixed, which is why different sized atoms distort the layers and make the alloy harder.

misconceptions.question: Is bronze copper and zinc?
misconceptions.correct: No. Bronze is copper and tin; brass is copper and zinc.
misconceptions.misconception: Bronze is the alloy of copper and zinc, and brass is the alloy of copper and tin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both alloys are copper based and both names are old and unhelpful, so the second metal is easy to swap over.
misconceptions.correction: Fix it by the pairing the specification gives: bronze - tin, brass - zinc. Brass instruments and door fittings are brass; statues and bells are bronze.

misconceptions.question: Are alloys softer than the pure metals they are made from?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alloys are usually harder, which is why most metals in everyday use are alloys.
misconceptions.misconception: Mixing metals dilutes them, so an alloy is always softer and weaker than a pure metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixing is associated with watering down, and the idea that pure means best carries over from everyday language.
misconceptions.correction: Pure metals have layers of identical atoms that slide easily. Different sized atoms in an alloy disrupt those layers, so alloys are usually harder than the pure metal.

misconceptions.question: Is jewellery gold pure gold?
misconceptions.correct: Usually not. It is normally an alloy of gold with silver, copper and zinc.
misconceptions.misconception: Gold jewellery is pure gold, and any other metal in it would be a fake.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Advertising treats 'pure gold' as the mark of quality, and carat numbers are read as a brand rather than a proportion.
misconceptions.correction: Pure gold is too soft for a ring worn every day. Silver, copper and zinc harden it, and the carat number states how much gold is present: 24 carat is 100%, 18 carat is 75%.

misconceptions.question: A ring is 18 carat. Is it 18% gold?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is 75% gold, because carats are measured out of 24 and 18 out of 24 is 75%.
misconceptions.misconception: The carat number is the percentage of gold, so 18 carat means 18% gold.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentages are the familiar scale, so an unfamiliar number is assumed to be one, and the fixed total of 24 is never noticed.
misconceptions.correction: The scale runs to 24, not to 100. Divide by 24: 24/24 is 100% and 18/24 is 75%. So 18 carat gold is three quarters gold.

misconceptions.question: Does more carbon make a steel softer?
misconceptions.correct: No. High carbon steel is strong but brittle; it is low carbon steel that is softer and more easily shaped.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon is a soft, crumbly non-metal, so the more carbon a steel contains the softer it becomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon is met as graphite in pencils, which is soft and slippery, and that image is transferred to steel.
misconceptions.correction: The carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and jam the layers so they cannot slide. That makes the steel hard and strong, but also brittle, so it snaps rather than bends.

misconceptions.question: Why does stainless steel resist corrosion?
misconceptions.correct: Because it contains chromium and nickel, which is what makes stainless steel hard and corrosion resistant.
misconceptions.misconception: Stainless steel resists rust because it is pure iron, or because of the carbon in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Stainless' sounds like clean and pure, and carbon is the only steel additive most students can name.
misconceptions.correction: Stainless steel is an alloy, not a pure metal, and the additions that matter are chromium and nickel. Carbon controls hardness and brittleness, not corrosion resistance.

misconceptions.question: Aluminium alloys are low density. Does that make them the strongest metals?
misconceptions.correct: No. Low density means a small mass for a given volume; it is a separate property from strength.
misconceptions.misconception: Low density is another way of saying very strong, so aluminium alloys must be stronger than steel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Aircraft are impressive and strong, so every property of the material used is assumed to be superior.
misconceptions.correction: Density and strength are different quantities. The reason aluminium alloys suit aircraft is that a given volume of them weighs less, so the plane is lighter to lift.

misconceptions.question: Does low density mean low mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. It means low mass for a given volume; a large aluminium part can still be heavy.
misconceptions.misconception: The denser a material is, the stronger and better it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density and mass are both about heaviness, and the 'per unit volume' half of the definition drops out.
misconceptions.correction: Density is mass divided by volume. A tonne of aluminium alloy still weighs a tonne, but it takes up far more room than a tonne of steel.

misconceptions.question: What is soda-lime glass made from?
misconceptions.correct: It is made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
misconceptions.misconception: Glass is just melted sand, so nothing else needs to be added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Demonstrations always stress that glass comes from sand, and the other two ingredients are less memorable.
misconceptions.correction: Sand alone melts only at a very high temperature. The specification gives three ingredients for soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.

misconceptions.question: Does borosilicate glass melt more easily than soda-lime glass?
misconceptions.correct: No. Borosilicate glass melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
misconceptions.misconception: Borosilicate glass melts at a lower temperature, which is why it is used for heating things.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Used in a Bunsen flame' gets muddled into 'melts easily', when the reason it is used there is the opposite.
misconceptions.correction: Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures. That is exactly why it survives being heated when ordinary glass would not.

misconceptions.question: How are clay ceramics made?
misconceptions.correct: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace.
misconceptions.misconception: Clay is melted and then poured into a mould, like molten glass or metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other shaping process the student has met - casting metals, moulding glass - starts by melting, so the same route is assumed for clay.
misconceptions.correction: Clay is shaped while it is wet and soft. Heating in a furnace afterwards is what hardens it permanently; it is never melted.

misconceptions.question: Are LD and HD poly(ethene) made from different monomers?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both are made from ethene; the catalyst and the conditions are what differ.
misconceptions.misconception: They must come from different monomers, because the two materials are so different.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Different product implies different starting material, which is usually a safe rule and fails here.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the properties of a polymer depend on the monomer AND on the conditions of manufacture. Same ethene, different catalyst and conditions, two different materials.

misconceptions.question: Do thermosetting polymers melt if you heat them enough?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything melts if it gets hot enough, so a thermosetting polymer just needs a higher temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Everything melts eventually' is a reasonable rule for simple molecular and metallic solids, and it is carried over without checking the structure.
misconceptions.correction: The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart. Heating strongly chars or burns the polymer; it does not melt and reshape.

misconceptions.question: Why does a thermosoftening polymer melt when heated?
misconceptions.correct: Its chains are separate and held to each other only by weak forces, so they can slide apart.
misconceptions.misconception: It melts because the strong covalent bonds along the polymer chains are broken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Melting is assumed to mean bond breaking, and the only bonds the student has labelled in the chain are the covalent ones.
misconceptions.correction: Melting separates chains from one another; it does not break the chains themselves. Only the weak forces between the tangled chains have to be overcome.

misconceptions.question: In a composite, which part surrounds which?
misconceptions.correct: The matrix or binder surrounds and binds together the reinforcement.
misconceptions.misconception: The fibres surround and hold the matrix in place.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reinforcement is named as the important part, so it is assumed to be the part on the outside doing the holding.
misconceptions.correction: The matrix is the continuous material - the cement in concrete, the resin in fibreglass. The reinforcement is the fibres or fragments held inside it.

misconceptions.question: Is a composite the same as an alloy?
misconceptions.correct: No. A composite has two separate materials, one held inside the other, and they stay distinct.
misconceptions.misconception: A composite is made by melting two materials together into one new substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both alloys and composites are 'two materials in one', so the more familiar alloy model is applied to both.
misconceptions.correction: In concrete you can still see the gravel in the cement. The two materials keep their own properties, which is what makes the combination useful.

misconceptions.question: Which sodium compound goes into soda-lime glass?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium carbonate. The mixture heated is sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium chloride is one of the ingredients of glass, because salt is the sodium compound you always meet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium chloride is by far the most familiar sodium compound, so it is substituted for the less familiar carbonate when the recipe is recalled.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names sodium carbonate. Sodium chloride is common salt and plays no part in making soda-lime glass; the third ingredient is limestone.

misconceptions.question: A material is picked because it is the strongest available. Is that enough?
misconceptions.correct: No. The choice must weigh every property the job needs, such as density, cost and resistance to corrosion.
misconceptions.misconception: The strongest material is always the best material to choose.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One property is easier to compare than several, so the comparison stops at the first number in the table.
misconceptions.correction: An aircraft body made of the strongest steel would be too heavy to fly. Selecting a material means matching all the properties to the use, which is why data tables give several columns.

misconceptions.question: Does 18 carat mean 18 parts of gold to 24 parts of other metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 24 is the whole, so 18 carat is 18 parts gold out of 24 parts of alloy, which is 75%.
misconceptions.misconception: The carat number and 24 are read as a ratio of gold to the other metals, rather than gold to the whole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ratios met in maths are usually part to part, like 3:2, so the fixed total of 24 is taken to be the other share instead of the total.
misconceptions.correction: Carats are a fraction of 24, not a ratio against 24. An 18 carat ring is 18/24 gold and 6/24 other metals, so 75% gold and 25% other metals.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by corrosion?

options.text: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with the environment
options.rationale: This is the specification definition: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.

options.text: Damage suffered only by metals, caused by oxygen in the air
options.rationale: Every worked example is a metal, so the general definition gets narrowed to metals only.

options.text: The rusting of iron that has been left outside in the wet
options.rationale: Rust is the only corrosion product students can name, so rusting is treated as the whole of corrosion.

options.text: The wearing away of a surface by scratching, rubbing and use
options.rationale: Corrosion is confused with mechanical wear, because both leave a surface eaten away, but corrosion is a chemical change.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?

options.text: Water alone; the air around the iron plays no part in it
options.rationale: Wetness is the visible change, so water is credited with the whole process.

options.text: Both air and water in contact with the iron surface
options.rationale: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

options.text: Air alone, since rust is simply an oxide of iron
options.rationale: The word oxide points to oxygen, so water is demoted to a helper rather than a necessity.

options.text: Salt water only, as pure water cannot rust iron
options.rationale: Seaside rusting is memorable, so salt is promoted from something that speeds rusting to something required for it.

mcqs.stem: A nail is put in a tube of water that has been boiled and then covered with a layer of oil. After a week the nail has not rusted. What does this show?

options.text: The layer of oil is what stopped the nail rusting here
options.rationale: Oil is a barrier method in this same topic, so it is mistaken for the variable being tested rather than the seal keeping air out.

options.text: Rusting needs only air, so the water was never needed
options.rationale: The result is read as evidence against water, when water is the one thing the tube does contain.

options.text: Water on its own cannot rust iron, so air is needed
options.rationale: Boiling drives dissolved air out and the oil stops it returning. The nail has water but no air and does not rust, so air is necessary as well.

options.text: A week is not long enough for rusting to be seen
options.rationale: A negative result is explained away by blaming the timescale instead of the variable that was removed.

mcqs.stem: A nail is sealed in a tube of air with anhydrous calcium chloride at the bottom. After a week it has not rusted. What does this show?

options.text: Calcium chloride is a chemical that prevents rust
options.rationale: Any added chemical is assumed to act on the nail itself, rather than to dry the air around it.

options.text: Air plays no part in the rusting of iron at all
options.rationale: The result is read as evidence against air, when air is the one thing this tube does contain.

options.text: Sealing up the tube is what kept the nail shiny here
options.rationale: The seal is treated as the cause, when its only job is to keep the tube's contents fixed.

options.text: Dry air cannot rust iron, so water is needed
options.rationale: The calcium chloride removes water vapour, so the nail has air but no water. It does not rust, so water is necessary as well.

mcqs.stem: Which method prevents corrosion by acting as a barrier?

options.text: Painting the surface so that air and water cannot reach the metal
options.rationale: Greasing, painting and electroplating are the barrier methods named by the specification; they keep air and water off the surface.

options.text: Bolting blocks of magnesium along the outside of the pipe
options.rationale: Sacrificial protection is a coating method too, so the two ways of protecting metal get merged.

options.text: Heating the metal strongly to harden its outside layer
options.rationale: Hardening is confused with protecting; a hard surface still reacts with air and water.

options.text: Mixing carbon into the metal to turn it into an alloy
options.rationale: Alloying changes the bulk properties of the metal, but it is not a coating and is not a barrier.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?

options.text: Aluminium is unreactive, so nothing in the air can attack it
options.rationale: The observation that it lasts is turned into a claim about reactivity that contradicts the reactivity series.

options.text: An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
options.rationale: Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.

options.text: Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh clean metal behind
options.rationale: Rust flakes off iron, so the same behaviour is assumed for aluminium oxide, which in fact stays put.

options.text: Frames are always painted before they are fitted
options.rationale: A real barrier method is offered, but it is not the reason the specification gives for aluminium.

mcqs.stem: Iron sheets are galvanised. What does this mean?

options.text: They are coated with tin, a metal that resists corrosion
options.rationale: Tin plating is a real process, but tin is less reactive than iron, so it is a barrier only.

options.text: They are dipped in acid to clean them before painting
options.rationale: An industrial pre-treatment is confused with the protective coating itself.

options.text: They are coated with zinc, which is more reactive
options.rationale: Galvanising is coating iron with zinc, a more reactive metal that gives sacrificial protection.

options.text: They are melted together with zinc as an alloy
options.rationale: Coating is confused with alloying; galvanising leaves a layer on the surface, it does not mix zinc through the iron.

mcqs.stem: A galvanised bucket is scratched right through to the iron. Why does the iron still not rust?

options.text: The zinc melts and seals the scratch up again
options.rationale: Zinc is credited with barrier behaviour only, so the gap has to be closed somehow for the iron to survive.

options.text: The iron corrodes first and so protects the zinc
options.rationale: The word sacrificial is attached to the metal being protected rather than to the coating doing the protecting.

options.text: The scratch is too narrow for water to get into
options.rationale: The protection is explained by geometry rather than by relative reactivity.

options.text: The zinc corrodes away in place of the iron
options.rationale: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead: sacrificial protection works even where the coating is broken.

mcqs.stem: Blocks of metal are bolted to a steel ship's hull to give sacrificial protection. Which metal should be used?

options.text: Magnesium, as it is more reactive than iron and corrodes first
options.rationale: Sacrificial protection needs a metal above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts in the iron's place.

options.text: Copper, because it is less reactive and resists corrosion
options.rationale: Resisting corrosion sounds like the property wanted, so the less reactive metal is chosen.

options.text: Tin, because it sits below iron and will not be eaten away
options.rationale: Tin plating is remembered as protection, but a less reactive metal cannot protect sacrificially.

options.text: Lead, because it is dense and very heavy for its size
options.rationale: A physical property is offered where a chemical one is needed; density has nothing to do with which metal corrodes.

mcqs.stem: Why are most metals in everyday use alloys rather than pure metals?

options.text: Alloys are compounds, so they cannot react with air at all
options.rationale: An alloy is treated as a compound, and a new substance is assumed to be unreactive.

options.text: The mixture has properties, like hardness, that suit the job
options.rationale: Most metals in everyday use are alloys because mixing gives more useful properties than the pure metal has.

options.text: Mixing metals always makes them much softer and easier to bend
options.rationale: Mixing is read as watering down, when different sized atoms in fact disrupt the layers and harden the metal.

options.text: Pure metals cost far too much to make in large amounts
options.rationale: Cost is a real factor in some cases, but it is not the property-based reason the specification gives.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about bronze is correct?

options.text: It is copper mixed with zinc in fixed amounts
options.rationale: Bronze and brass are both copper based, so the second metal is easily swapped over.

options.text: It is a compound formed from copper and tin
options.rationale: The right two metals are named, but mixing is confused with chemical combination.

options.text: It is an alloy of copper mixed with tin
options.rationale: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

options.text: It is a pure metal mined as bronze ore
options.rationale: An alloy is treated as an element, as though bronze came out of the ground ready made.

mcqs.stem: Brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings. What is brass?

options.text: A mixture of copper and pure tin
options.rationale: The alloy pairs are swapped: copper and tin is bronze, not brass.

options.text: A compound of copper and zinc
options.rationale: The right metals are named, but an alloy is a mixture, not a compound with a fixed formula.

options.text: Iron with a thin copper coating
options.rationale: A coated metal is confused with an alloy; brass is mixed throughout, not plated.

options.text: A mixture of copper and zinc
options.rationale: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which is why it is used for instruments and fittings.

mcqs.stem: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy. Which metals is the gold usually mixed with?

options.text: The gold is mixed with silver, copper and zinc
options.rationale: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc.

options.text: Nothing else, since jewellery gold is pure
options.rationale: Pure gold is treated as the mark of quality, so the idea of an alloy is rejected.

options.text: Iron and carbon, added to harden the gold
options.rationale: The recipe for steel is transferred to gold, because hardening is the correct reason for alloying.

options.text: A compound of gold, silver, copper and zinc
options.rationale: The right metals are named, but an alloy is a mixture of elements, not a compound formed by a reaction.

mcqs.stem: A ring is stamped 18 carat. What does this tell you about the ring?

options.text: It contains 18% gold and 82% of other metals
options.rationale: The carat number is read as a percentage, because percentages are the familiar scale.

options.text: It is 75% gold, because 24 carat means pure gold
options.rationale: Carats are measured out of 24, so 18 carat is 18/24, which is 75% gold.

options.text: It is pure gold and it weighs 18 carats on a balance
options.rationale: Carat is taken to be a unit of mass, and the alloy idea is dropped altogether.

options.text: It has 18 parts of gold to 24 parts of other metal
options.rationale: The 24 is read as the share of other metal instead of the total number of parts, so the ratio is set up part to part.

mcqs.stem: How does high carbon steel differ from low carbon steel?

options.text: High carbon steel is soft and easy to shape; low carbon steel is brittle
options.rationale: Carbon is met as soft graphite, so more carbon is assumed to mean a softer steel. The two descriptions are the wrong way round.

options.text: High carbon steel resists corrosion; low carbon steel rusts very fast
options.rationale: Carbon is credited with corrosion resistance, which in fact comes from chromium and nickel.

options.text: High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer
options.rationale: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, while low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped.

options.text: High carbon steel is a compound; low carbon steel is a mixture
options.rationale: Believing alloys are compounds, the student treats the higher-carbon steel as the chemically combined compound.

mcqs.stem: Why is stainless steel chosen for cutlery and sinks?

options.text: It is pure iron, so there is nothing to rust
options.rationale: The word stainless is read as pure, when stainless steel is in fact an alloy.

options.text: It has extra carbon in it, which stops any rust
options.rationale: Carbon is the only steel additive many students can name, so it is credited with the corrosion resistance.

options.text: It is soft, so it can be pressed into thin sheets
options.rationale: A property of low carbon steel is transferred to stainless steel, and softness would be no use in a knife.

options.text: It is hard and it resists corrosion well
options.rationale: Steels containing chromium and nickel are hard and resistant to corrosion.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium alloys are used for the bodies of aircraft. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are low density, so a given volume of them weighs less
options.rationale: Aluminium alloys are low density, so an aircraft body made from them is lighter to lift.

options.text: They are the strongest metals known, so they never bend
options.rationale: Low density is read as a claim about strength, when the two properties are separate.

options.text: They are dense, so they are tough enough for an aircraft.
options.rationale: Density is confused with mass; a large aluminium alloy part is still heavy.

options.text: They melt easily, so parts can be cast into shape
options.rationale: Ease of manufacture is offered instead of the property in service; a body that melted easily would be a poor choice.

mcqs.stem: Duralumin is an alloy of aluminium with copper and magnesium. Its density is 2.8 g/cm3 and it is harder than pure aluminium. A titanium alloy has a density of 4.5 g/cm3 and is harder than duralumin. Which is the better choice for a lightweight bicycle frame that must not bend?

options.text: Titanium alloy, because it is the harder of the two
options.rationale: One column of the table decides the answer; the density figures, which the question is about, are ignored.

options.text: Duralumin, because it is far less dense and still hard
options.rationale: The frame must be light, and 2.8 g/cm3 is well below 4.5 g/cm3, while duralumin is still harder than pure aluminium.

options.text: Titanium alloy, because a denser metal is always stronger
options.rationale: Density is treated as a measure of strength; the two are different quantities.

options.text: Pure aluminium, because it is stronger than any alloy
options.rationale: Believing alloying always weakens a metal, the student picks pure aluminium as the strongest choice.

mcqs.stem: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?

options.text: Sand with boron trioxide, heated strongly
options.rationale: This is the recipe for borosilicate glass, which the specification lists separately.

options.text: Sand on its own, melted in a hot furnace
options.rationale: Glass is remembered as melted sand, and the other two ingredients drop out.

options.text: Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
options.rationale: Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.

options.text: Clay, limestone and sodium chloride
options.rationale: Clay belongs to ceramics, and sodium chloride is confused with sodium carbonate.

mcqs.stem: How does borosilicate glass differ from soda-lime glass?

options.text: It melts at a much lower temperature
options.rationale: Its use in heated glassware is muddled into melting easily, when the reason is the opposite.

options.text: It is made from pure sand and nothing else
options.rationale: Believing glass is only melted sand, the student thinks borosilicate contains sand alone.

options.text: It melts easily once it gets hot enough
options.rationale: Believing everything melts if hot enough, the student expects borosilicate to melt readily.

options.text: It melts at a higher temperature
options.rationale: Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

mcqs.stem: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?

options.text: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace
options.rationale: Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating in a furnace.

options.text: Clay is melted and poured into a cold mould
options.rationale: Casting is the shaping route the student knows for metals and glass, so it is assumed for clay too.

options.text: Dry clay powder is pressed and left to set
options.rationale: The heating step is dropped, which is the step that makes the change permanent.

options.text: Clay is mixed with sand and melted down
options.rationale: The recipe for glass is transferred to ceramics.

mcqs.stem: LD and HD poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. Why do they have different properties?

options.text: They are built from two different monomers
options.rationale: A different product is assumed to need a different starting material, but both come from ethene.

options.text: A different catalyst and conditions are used
options.rationale: The properties of polymers depend on the monomer and on the conditions under which they are made, so the same ethene gives two different materials.

options.text: HD poly(ethene) is pressed hard after it is made
options.rationale: The word density is taken literally as compression, rather than as a property that follows from how the polymer was made.

options.text: The HD chains contain a second element
options.rationale: An extra element is invented to explain the difference; both polymers are made from ethene alone.

mcqs.stem: Why do thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated?

options.text: The strong covalent bonds along the chains break
options.rationale: Melting is assumed to mean bond breaking, and the covalent bonds are the only ones labelled in the chain.

options.text: Any solid will melt if it is heated enough
options.rationale: Believing everything melts if hot enough, the student attributes melting to heat alone, ignoring weak forces.

options.text: Separate chains are held only by weak forces
options.rationale: The chains are separate and tangled, with only weak forces between them, so they slide apart when heated.

options.text: The polymer is a liquid that was frozen
options.rationale: Melting is explained as reversing freezing, which ignores the structure of the polymer altogether.

mcqs.stem: Why do thermosetting polymers keep their shape when they are heated?

options.text: They only melt above about a thousand degrees
options.rationale: The rule that everything melts eventually is carried over without checking the structure.

options.text: The covalent bonds in the chains never break
options.rationale: Believing melting means chain covalent bonds break, the student thinks unbroken bonds keep the shape.

options.text: They contain no carbon that could be melted
options.rationale: Melting is confused with burning away, and every polymer is built on carbon chains.

options.text: Cross-links join the chains to each other
options.rationale: The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart and the polymer does not melt.

mcqs.stem: Most composites are made of two materials. How are those two materials arranged?

options.text: A matrix surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments
options.rationale: Most composites are made of a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the reinforcement.

options.text: Two materials are melted into a single new substance
options.rationale: The alloy model is applied to composites; in a composite the two materials stay distinct.

options.text: Fibres surround the matrix and hold it firmly in place
options.rationale: The roles are reversed: the reinforcement is named as the important part, so it is put on the outside.

options.text: Two elements are joined chemically to give a compound
options.rationale: A composite is not a compound; nothing reacts and the parts can still be seen.

mcqs.stem: Which of these materials is a composite?

options.text: Brass, which is copper mixed with zinc
options.rationale: An alloy is a mixture of metals, not a matrix holding a reinforcement.

options.text: Concrete, gravel held together by cement
options.rationale: Concrete is a composite: cement is the matrix and the gravel is the reinforcement.

options.text: Poly(ethene), made from many ethene units
options.rationale: A polymer is one material made of long chains, not two materials combined.

options.text: Soda-lime glass, made by melting sand
options.rationale: Glass is a single material made by heating a mixture of ingredients until they react and fuse.

mcqs.stem: A table gives: aluminium alloy, density 2.7 g/cm3, does not shatter; soda-lime glass, density 2.5 g/cm3, shatters when dropped; carbon fibre composite, density 1.6 g/cm3, does not shatter. Which material is lightest for a given volume and survives being dropped?

options.text: Soda-lime glass, since glass is the lightest here
options.rationale: The density column is misread and the shattering column is ignored; glass is not the least dense material listed.

options.text: Aluminium alloy, since a metal can never break
options.rationale: One property, toughness, decides the answer and the density figures are not used at all.

options.text: The carbon fibre composite, the least dense
options.rationale: At 1.6 g/cm3 it is the least dense of the three, and the table says it does not shatter.

options.text: Aluminium alloy, as it is the densest one
options.rationale: Density is treated as a measure of quality, and the question asked for the lightest for a given volume.

mcqs.stem: A saucepan handle must not soften on the hot hob and must not conduct heat well. Which material is most suitable?

options.text: A polymer with strong covalent chains
options.rationale: Believing melting needs breaking strong covalent chains, the student wrongly expects heat resistance on the hob.

options.text: A toughened soda-lime glass
options.rationale: Glass copes with the heat but shatters when a pan is knocked, so it is a poor choice for a handle.

options.text: A hard-wearing steel alloy
options.rationale: Hardness is chosen as the deciding property, but a metal handle conducts heat straight to the hand.

options.text: A thermosetting polymer
options.rationale: Thermosetting polymers do not melt when heated and, being polymers, are poor conductors of heat.

mcqs.stem: Which object is most likely to be made from bronze?

options.text: A church bell cast in one piece
options.rationale: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, is used for bells, statues and ornaments.

options.text: A trumpet played in a school band
options.rationale: Bronze and brass are swapped, so the brass instrument is picked for bronze.

options.text: A knife blade that stays sharp
options.rationale: Blades are high carbon steel, which is strong and hard enough to hold an edge.

options.text: A drinks can pressed from thin sheet
options.rationale: Cans are aluminium alloy, chosen because it is low density and easily shaped.

mcqs.stem: What is high carbon steel used for?

options.text: Car body panels and sheeting
options.rationale: More carbon is assumed to make the steel softer, so the easily shaped use is chosen.

options.text: Cutlery and kitchen sinks
options.rationale: Carbon is credited with resisting corrosion, so the corrosion resistant use is chosen.

options.text: Cutting tools and sharp blades
options.rationale: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, which suits cutting tools and blades.

options.text: Aeroplane bodies and frames
options.rationale: Aircraft bodies use aluminium alloys, because those are low density.
